memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: He must acknowledge the son of his unloved wife as the firstborn by giving him a double share of all he has. That son is the first sign of his father's strength. The right of the firstborn belongs to him. - Deut 21:17 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
God insists that the true firstborn receive his rightful double portion, regardless of the father's personal feelings. The firstborn was described as "the first sign of his father's strength," and his rights were to be honoured. God would not allow the rightful claim to be set aside because of a parent's changing affections.

This law upholds a principle of integrity, honouring what is rightly due to someone, even when our feelings might lead us elsewhere. Rights and responsibilities are not to be governed by favouritism or convenience, but by what is just and true. God builds fairness into the very fabric of family life.

There is a beautiful gospel echo here too. In Christ, believers are brought into an inheritance we did not earn. Jesus is the true firstborn over all creation, and through Him we become co-heirs, receiving a rich inheritance by grace (Rom 8:17). We who deserved nothing are given everything in Christ, not because of favouritism, but because of God's lavish grace poured out through His Son. The God who insisted on honouring rightful claims has, in Christ, granted us a claim to glory we could never deserve. As you consider your inheritance in Christ, does gratitude fill your heart, and does that gratitude make you fair and generous toward others?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you honour what is rightly due to others, even against your feelings?
2. How does your inheritance in Christ stir gratitude in you?
3. How can gratitude make you more fair and generous?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, thank You for the undeserved inheritance I have in Christ. Fill me with gratitude, and make me fair and generous toward others. Amen.
